content.title: About
content.content: Toasted bread with raisins is a whole‑grain loaf that contains raisins in the dough and is then sliced and toasted until the crust turns golden. It offers a sweet raisin aroma, a crunchy texture, and a mildly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Toasting enhances the aroma and creates a crisp crust.
Raisins retain some of their antioxidants even after heating.
This type of bread is traditional in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines.
The sweet raisins paired with slightly salty bread make it a popular breakfast or snack.
Toasted raisin bread is often served with butter, honey, or cheese.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread and raisins are rich in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Raisins provide iron that contributes to normal hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Raisins contain flavonoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bread and natural sugars from raisins give a quick source of energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The bread supplies B1, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins raise the sugar level, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Toasted raisin bread is relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy toasted raisin bread as a snack on its own, spread with butter, honey, or cream cheese, or use it for sandwiches with ham, cheese, or avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer storage, refrigerate, where it stays fresh for up to 2 weeks.

frozen-coffee-drink-with-non-dairy-milk-.title: Frozen Coffee Drink with Non-Dairy Milk and Whipped Cream

content.title: About
content.content: A frozen coffee drink with non-dairy milk and whipped cream is a refreshing dessert‑style beverage made from cold espresso, plant‑based milk (soy, almond, oat) and a thick dollop of dairy‑free whipped cream. Served as a dense frappe, it is often topped with sprinkles or chocolate shavings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first frozen coffee drinks appeared in Italy in the 1950s under the name "caffè freddo".
Plant‑based milks allow lactose‑intolerant consumers to enjoy the drink without compromising flavor.
Dairy‑free whipped cream is frequently made from coconut cream, which whips into a stable foam.
The drink is a staple of summer menus worldwide because of its cooling texture.
Numerous flavor variations exist: vanilla, caramel, mint, and seasonal additions like pumpkin spice.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Using plant‑based milk eliminates lactose, making the beverage safe for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Espresso provides polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Coffee contains vitamins B2, B3, and B5, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats from plant milk
items.content: Soy, almond, or oat milks contain mono‑ and polyunsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Coconut cream and MCTs
items.content: If the whipped cream is made from coconut cream, it supplies medium‑chain triglycerides that are quickly used for energy.

items.title: Nut or soy allergy
items.content: Plant milks are often derived from soy, almonds, or cashews; allergic individuals should check ingredients.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Syrups or added sugar are common for sweetness, which can raise calorie count and affect blood glucose.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Espresso contains caffeine, which may cause insomnia or increased anxiety in sensitive people.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Dairy‑free whipped cream, especially from coconut, can be calorie‑rich; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the drink in tall glasses, garnish with whipped cream, a dusting of cocoa powder or chocolate shavings. For extra richness, add a scoop of dairy‑free ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The beverage is best enjoyed immediately. If stored, keep it refrigerated for no more than 2‑3 hours; the whipped cream may separate, so give it a quick re‑whip before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Onion dip made with yogurt is a smooth sauce that combines fresh onion, natural yogurt, and spices. It offers a light tang, aromatic onion flavor, and creamy texture, making it a perfect accompaniment for veggie sticks, chips, sandwiches, and grilled dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yogurt‑based dip is often used instead of sour cream to lower calories and add probiotics.
Onion retains beneficial compounds such as quercetin, an antioxidant.
The onion‑yogurt combination is traditional in Mediterranean cuisine.
The dip can be customized with fresh herbs, garlic, or hot sauce.
Both regular and Greek yogurt can be used, altering thickness and protein content.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Yogurt provides live bacterial cultures that support gut health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with traditional creamy dips, the yogurt version usually contains less saturated fat.

items.title: Vitamin B12 and calcium
items.content: Yogurt is a source of vitamin B12 and calcium, important for bones and nervous system.

items.title: Onion antioxidants
items.content: Onion is rich in quercetin and sulfur compounds that may reduce inflammation.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Greek yogurt boosts the protein content, helping increase satiety.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy should choose a dairy‑free alternative or use plant‑based yogurt.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared dip may contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should use it sparingly.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The yogurt makes the dip more acidic, which can cause discomfort for sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Because of fresh ingredients, the dip should be kept refrigerated and consumed within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip chilled with fresh vegetable sticks, potato wedges, crackers, as a sauce for burgers, in wraps, or as a salad dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. It keeps for 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops off‑smell or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork sausage (item 990) is a ready‑to‑eat meat product made from ground pork, fat, salt and spices. It is usually thermally processed (boiled, smoked or baked) and packaged as whole links or sliced sausages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally pork sausage is formed into long links or round sticks.
Common spices include black pepper, garlic, paprika and nutmeg.
Smoking gives a distinctive aroma and extends shelf life.
Many countries have their own versions: German Bratwurst, Polish Kielbasa, American Hot Dog.
Sausage can be sold fresh (requiring further cooking) or pre‑cooked and ready to eat.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Pork sausage provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B1, B3 and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: The product supplies iron and zinc, important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Its fat content makes it a quick source of calories.

items.title: High salt content
items.content: Large amounts of salt can raise blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Sausage is rich in saturated fats, which may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some varieties contain nitrites that can form potentially harmful compounds during long storage.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to pork or added ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sausage can be eaten cold as a slice, pan‑fried, boiled in soups, or used in dishes such as pasta, casseroles and salads. Before cooking, heat to an internal temperature of at least 70 °C.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sausage in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Fresh links keep for up to 5 days, smoked varieties up to 2 weeks. When frozen (‑18 °C) they can be kept for 2–3 months. Discard any product with off‑odors or discoloration.

salisbury-steak-with-gravy-whipped-potat.title: Salisbury steak with gravy, whipped potatoes, vegetable, dessert (frozen meal)

content.title: About
content.content: Salisbury steak with gravy is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal that includes a seasoned ground‑beef patty in a tomato‑based gravy, whipped potatoes, a vegetable side (usually carrots and peas), and a sweet dessert such as fruit jelly. The portion is designed for a single serving and can be reheated in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first frozen meals appeared in the United States in the 1950s, and the Salisbury steak version became popular in the 1970s.
The dish is named after Dr. James H. Salisbury, who promoted a meat‑based diet in the early 20th century.
The gravy typically contains tomato paste, onion, garlic, and spices like paprika and black pepper.
The whipped potatoes are made from selected potatoes, butter, and a splash of milk, giving them a light, airy texture.
The dessert is often a fruit‑flavored jelly that retains its bright color and flavor even after freezing.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The beef patty provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and gravy supply vitamin B12 and niacin, supporting nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Potassium from potatoes
items.content: Whipped potatoes are a good source of potassium, which helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: The vegetable side adds dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Natural fruit sugars in dessert
items.content: The fruit jelly dessert provides a modest amount of vitamin C and antioxidants.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The prepared gravy can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should limit the portion.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: To ensure shelf stability, the meal may contain preservatives that some sensitive individuals prefer to avoid.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Although rare, an allergy to beef or specific spices in the gravy can occur.

items.title: Need for thorough heating
items.content: Insufficient heating may leave harmful bacteria; follow the heating instructions carefully.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Defrost the package in the microwave or on the stovetop, heat until steaming hot, stir the steak with its gravy, and serve alongside the whipped potatoes, vegetables, and dessert. Garnish with fresh herbs or grated cheese if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen meal at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once opened, store any leftovers in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days and reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Samosa is a traditional pastry made of dough, usually filled with meat, potatoes, onions and spices. The dough can be flaky or yeasted, and the filling varies by region. Samosas are popular in Central Asian, Indian and Balkan cuisines, often served hot as a snack or a main dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “samosa” comes from the Persian “samsa”, meaning “triangular”.
In different countries the shape can be triangular, half‑moon or square.
Traditionally samosas are baked in a tandoor – a clay oven – which gives them a distinctive aroma and crisp crust.
Some regions add pumpkin, peas or cheese to the filling, creating vegetarian versions.
Samosas are often served with a hot chili sauce or a yogurt‑based dip to balance the spiciness.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat fillings provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat in the filling is a good source of heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Both the dough and meat contain B1, B3 and B6 vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used, the pastry adds dietary fiber that helps digestion.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbs and fats makes samosa a quick source of energy, useful before physical activity.

items.title: High in fat and calories
items.content: Flaky dough and fatty fillings make samosas calorie‑dense, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or E. coli.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Fillings are often salty; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional dough contains wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Samosas are usually eaten hot, cut into bite‑size pieces. They can be served with spicy chutney, tomato sauce or a simple yogurt dip. Cold samosas are also popular as a portable snack for picnics.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked samosas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag; thaw at room temperature before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Stew, chicken, with pasta is a dish where bite‑size pieces of chicken breast are slowly cooked in a flavorful broth together with pasta, vegetables, and spices. The dish combines the tenderness of chicken, the heartiness of pasta, and the depth of seasoned broth, making it popular both at home and in restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewing helps retain maximum flavor and nutrients in the chicken meat.
Pasta absorbs part of the broth, becoming more aromatic.
Short‑shaped pasta such as penne or farfalle is traditionally used because it holds the sauce better.
The dish is often finished with a sprinkle of fresh parsley or grated Parmesan cheese.
In some regional recipes, tomato paste is added for a brighter color and a hint of acidity.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta supplies sustained energy through complex carbs.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and whole‑grain pasta are good sources of B6 and B12, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc, and magnesium, important for immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using skinless chicken and moderate oil keeps the dish relatively low in saturated fats.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C to eliminate salmonella and other pathogens.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared broths or soy sauce can raise sodium levels; homemade broth is a healthier option.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives should be used for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: The dish can become calorie‑dense with large amounts of pasta and oil; mindful portion sizes are recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot, garnished with fresh herbs. Add grated cheese, a drizzle of olive oil, or a squeeze of lemon juice for extra brightness. The dish stores well in the refrigerator and can be reheated in the microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.

tea-iced-instant-black-decaffeinated-uns.title: Tea, iced, instant, black, decaffeinated, unsweetened

content.title: About
content.content: Iced instant black tea, decaffeinated and unsweetened, is a convenient beverage that prepares quickly, retains the characteristic flavor of black tea, but contains no stimulating caffeine. Ideal for those who want a refreshing drink without extra calories or stimulants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is the most consumed tea worldwide after green tea.
Decaffeination is usually done with water or CO₂, preserving most aromatic compounds.
Instant tea was invented in the early 20th century and became popular for its speed of preparation.
Unsweetened, this tea has virtually zero calories, making it diet‑friendly.
Iced tea is often served with ice and a slice of lemon for extra flavor.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Black tea is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular tea consumption may improve vascular function.

items.title: Caffeine‑free hydration
items.content: The lack of caffeine makes it safe for evening consumption without sleep disruption.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Without added sugar, the tea contains virtually no calories.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Tannins in black tea can help normalize stomach function.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Tannin content
items.content: High amounts of tannins can reduce iron absorption from foods.

items.title: Microplastic presence
items.content: Some packaging may contain microplastics; choose reputable brands.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dissolve 1‑2 teaspoons of powder in 250 ml of cold water, add ice, and optionally a lemon slice or mint. It can also serve as a base for cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the packet in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Vinegar is a liquid produced by the fermentation of sugars into acetic acid. Common types include apple cider, wine, distilled (grain‑based) and balsamic. It is used as a culinary seasoning, preservative and cleaning agent.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest recorded vinegar recipe comes from ancient Egypt, around 3000 BC.
Apple cider vinegar is often called “natural” because it undergoes double fermentation: sugars become alcohol, then acetic acid.
Balsamic vinegar was originally made in Italy for over 800 years and aged in wooden barrels for up to 25 years.
Vinegar can be used to test pH at home: its reaction with indicator solutions shows acidity.
In some cultures vinegar is regarded as a longevity tonic due to its antioxidant properties.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar, especially apple cider, may stimulate gastric juice production, aiding food breakdown.

items.title: Blood sugar regulation
items.content: Moderate vinegar intake has been shown to lower post‑prandial glucose spikes.

items.title: Antibacterial properties
items.content: Acetic acid can inhibit the growth of certain bacteria and fungi, making vinegar an effective preservative.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Some studies suggest vinegar may help reduce LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Weight management aid
items.content: Vinegar can increase feelings of fullness, helping control calorie intake.

items.title: Mucosal irritation
items.content: The acidity of vinegar can cause burning or irritation of the stomach and esophagus when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Vinegar may potentiate the effects of diuretics and blood‑glucose‑lowering medications.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Frequent undiluted vinegar consumption can wear down tooth enamel.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may react to components present in fermented products.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add vinegar to marinades, sauces, salad dressings and pickled vegetables. For preserving, dilute it with water (commonly 1:1). Small amounts enhance the flavor of dishes, and a diluted solution works well for cleaning surfaces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store vinegar in a tightly sealed glass or plastic bottle in a cool, dark place. Properly stored, it remains stable for years. Discard if it becomes cloudy, develops sediment, or changes smell.
